title: Exhalation — Begin With Moving Air
learningGoals: Recognise a held or pressured start
Explore a short message without breath exhaustion

sections.heading: Welcome and what we will explore
sections.narration:
Welcome. Today we are exploring Exhalation — Begin With Moving Air. Beginning a sentence feels like a held starting gate. You want to ask a simple question, but extra preparation can become another task.

We will recognise a held or pressured start, observe comfortable outward airflow, and explore a short message without breath exhaustion. First I will explain the distinction. Then you will see and hear a demonstration, try a few short phrases, and notice your own experience. We will finish with a short prepared rehearsal and an everyday next step. You can pause or ask a question at any point. A small comfortable experiment is enough.

sections.heading: What this tool means
sections.narration:
Airflow is the movement of air. Voice onset is when voiced sound begins, and articulation is how the mouth shapes sounds. They work together, but this lesson gives attention to airflow rather than asking you to manage all three at once.

Before a first word, you may notice that you hold your breath or add pressure. Today we will explore the beginning of a message with comfortable moving air. This is a physical exploration, not a requirement to arrange a perfect breath before every sentence. Let breathing remain comfortable, and use short phrases with time to breathe again.

Notice the distinction: The focus is comfortable moving air, not a large inhalation or exhausting the breath. You are choosing one feature for this learning experience, rather than inspecting every aspect of speech. We will use short familiar messages so there is room to notice that feature.

sections.heading: Watch and listen
sections.narration:
Watch the demonstration before trying. We will use this message: I would like some water. First listen to the models and notice the feature being compared. The labels on screen identify each version. You can replay either model without copying an uncomfortable contrast.

Now listen once more for the message itself. Whether beginning felt held, pressured or easier; whether breath remained comfortable. This is an invitation to compare your experience, not a demand to match the model exactly. When you are ready, move to a short guided attempt.

sections.heading: Try the three small steps
sections.narration:
Let us try this in small steps. First: Notice a comfortable breath without trying to enlarge it. Next: Try a short familiar phrase while allowing outward airflow. Then: Pause naturally and compare another short phrase.

Use these familiar phrases one at a time: I would like some water. The meeting starts tomorrow. Can I ask a question? Stop between attempts when you want to. You can listen to a model again, record a short attempt, or leave this part to return later. Keep attention on this one chosen feature; you do not need to check every sound. If the attempt becomes effortful, stop and return to comfortable ordinary speaking.

sections.heading: Compare and check
sections.narration:
Consider what this tool is asking you to explore. What is the purpose of this airflow exploration? You can select an answer and read or hear the explanation. It is a check of the idea, not a test of how you sound.

After the check, notice one observation from your attempt: Whether beginning felt held, pressured or easier; whether breath remained comfortable. It is possible for a movement to feel different while the message still takes effort, or for you to be unsure what changed. You can record that uncertainty without repeating until you obtain a preferred result.

sections.heading: From a phrase to your own message
sections.narration:
Choose a short message you actually want to share. You might use one of the phrases we have practised and add one useful detail in your own words. Give yourself one small cue from the demonstration, then let the message continue. There is no need to increase the amount of the technique to make the attempt count.

After speaking, ask what you noticed about the chosen feature and about the message. You can keep a small useful change, adjust it, or leave the result open. Try another short message only if it serves your learning today.

sections.heading: Your observation and next step
sections.narration:
Before finishing, save one observation. Here is the feature we explored: Whether beginning felt held, pressured or easier; whether breath remained comfortable. Something may have changed, things may have felt much the same, or you may be unsure. Your observation belongs to this attempt and setting.

In focused practice, you can deliberately explore this one feature. In conversation, give most of your attention to the message and the other person. A familiar support can be available if it helps; it does not need to become a checklist you monitor throughout the exchange.

Choose one manageable situation in which you would like to speak. You can plan a small practice, have a conversation, revisit the demonstration, or finish here. Save what you would keep, change or leave open.
